title: Only now
hook: each lives only this moment; the rest is gone or unknown (Meditations 3.10)

segments.voice: Yesterday: honor the power of judgment. Your line was judge carefully. When a verdict popped up, did you catch the gap between what you saw and what you decided? Day five hundred forty-five.

Where are you right now? Not where your body is. Where your mind is. For many of us, at any given moment, it's replaying a conversation from Tuesday or rehearsing one for Friday. We carry the past like a backpack and the future like a weather forecast, and we barely glance at the one place we actually stand. Marcus Aurelius, writing in a camp on the frontier, with war behind him and more war ahead, set all of that down in a few short lines. Today: only now.
screen: `WHERE IS YOUR MIND?` → `TUESDAY BEHIND, FRIDAY AHEAD.` → `ONLY NOW.`

segments.voice: First, throw the rest away. Marcus opens the tenth entry of book three by telling himself to let everything else go and hold on to these few things. It's a clearing-out. Second, the moment. Each of us, he says, lives only the present, this moment that can't be divided. Everything else is either already lived or uncertain. That's not a mood. It's a description. You cannot live yesterday again, and you cannot yet live tomorrow. The only life anyone actually has is happening in this breath. Third, how small it all is. Then Marcus widens the lens. Short is the life each person lives. Small is the corner of the earth where they live it. Short, too, is the longest fame after death, and it's passed along by people who will die soon themselves, who don't know even themselves, let alone someone long gone. He's not trying to depress himself. He's pulling his attention back from the places it wanders, the regrets and the legacy, to the one place it can do any good. Fourth, why this is freedom. If the past is finished and the future unknown, then neither one is where your choices happen. The present is small, but it's the only part of life you can steer. Marcus wasn't the only one to notice. Many contemplative traditions teach some form of returning to this moment, each in its own words. For Marcus, it's plain arithmetic: the present is all anyone loses, and all anyone has.
screen: `THROW THE REST AWAY.` · `EACH LIVES ONLY THIS MOMENT.` · `SHORT LIFE, SMALL CORNER, SHORT FAME.` · `THE ONLY PART YOU CAN STEER.` · then, large: `ONLY THIS.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Feel this breath: the cool air coming in, the slight warmth going out. That's it. That's the whole of your life right now. When your mind drifts to earlier today, notice it, and say quietly, gone. When it drifts to later, notice it, and say, unknown. Then come back to this breath. And this one. Only this. The bell holds the time.
Only now. Marcus says each person lives only this moment; the past is already lived, and the future is uncertain. Today's word.
Your line: only this. Three times today, when your mind runs ahead or behind, feel one breath and say: only this. Day five hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often return to Meditations 3.10 when worry or regret pulls at them, bringing their attention back to the present moment as the only part of life they can act in.

original.note: Greek, 'the present': the moment Marcus says is all each of us lives.

trapdoor: what you thought: live in the moment.
what it means: the past is finished, the future unknown; this moment is the only place your choices happen.
what a scholar hears: the Stoics treated the present as the only time a person can lose, a theme Marcus returns to in 2.14 as well.

notes: 3.10 paraphrased: throw away all else and hold to these few things; each lives only the present, which is an indivisible point; the rest is either lived or uncertain; short the life, small the corner of earth, short the longest posthumous fame, passed on by poor men who die soon and know not themselves, much less one long dead. Confirm.
Marcus 'writing in a camp on the frontier': Book 3 carries a heading placing it at Carnuntum in most manuscripts. Confirm the heading and its reliability.
Trapdoor cites 2.14 (the present is all a man can lose); confirm.
Greek 'to paron': confirm the phrase as used in 3.10.
